# A Call to Action for the Architecture 2.0 Ecosystem {#sec-bootstrapping-ecosystem}

::: {.epigraph}
> *"Organizing complexity through shared design rules and standard abstractions allowed an entire generation of engineers to build systems of unprecedented scale."*
>
> — Carver Mead and Lynn Conway, *Introduction to VLSI Systems* (1980) [@MeadConway1980VLSI]
:::

::: {.column-margin}
**Author's Note.** Carver Mead and Lynn Conway transformed semiconductor design by establishing scalable abstractions and shared design rules that decoupled logic design from fabrication physics. In Architecture 2.0, our challenge is to create open schemas, open signoff stacks, neutral benchmark rules, and competitive grand challenges that decouple autonomous search loops from proprietary CAD lock-in.
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
How can open data standards, open PDK signoff stacks, neutral consortium benchmarks, and competitive grand challenges be coordinated to transform AI-native hardware exploration into a trusted, auditable engineering discipline across the industry?
:::

Building a discipline-wide ecosystem for autonomous computer architecture requires us to coordinate action across industry, academia, funding agencies, standards bodies, and tooling vendors. In Architecture 1.0, microarchitectural exploration relied on hand-crafted Hardware Description Language (HDL) modules, manual design space sweeps, and monolithic Electronic Design Automation (EDA) licenses. In Architecture 2.0, autonomous search loops and generative models explore vast design spaces dynamically. Just as VLSI co-design, deep learning benchmarking, and open instruction set architectures required shared foundations, our discipline demands open data standards, open signoff harnesses, neutral governance, and competitive grand challenges to transform AI-native hardware exploration into an auditable engineering discipline.

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}
This chapter achieves the following learning objectives.

- Sequence the six master staging steps required to construct an open Architecture 2.0 ecosystem.
- Formulate open schema protocols and cryptographic attempt lineage headers for agentic hardware tools.
- Establish neutral consortium benchmark governance and public failure repository indexing.
- Deploy open companion hub resources, reference audit tools, and containerized design starter kits.
:::

## Ecosystem Staging and Execution Sequence {#sec-staging-sequence}

When we deploy autonomous search loops into hardware design without shared infrastructure, we risk compounding system fragmentation rather than accelerating progress. Building a resilient engineering ecosystem demands that we carefully stage our investments, ensuring that foundational data schemas and physical signoff harnesses precede the deployment of generative models or unconstrained design space exploration.

Six sequential steps establish this shared engineering infrastructure (@tbl-ecosystem-staging-sequence). Foundational open process design kit (PDK) data schemas and physical signoff harnesses anchor the early steps before the discipline advances to consortium governance, grand challenges, public failure repositories, and workforce badging.

| **Step** | **Ecosystem action** | **Primary deliverable** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Step 1 | Shared Data Schemas and Tool Contracts | Open schemas for prompt logs, tool flags, ASTs, CDFGs, and container execution environments |
| Step 2 | Open PDKs and Cloud Silicon Shuttles | Open PDK access (Sky130/ASAP7) and cloud shuttle passes with OpenROAD/OpenSTA physical signoff telemetry |
| Step 3 | Consortium Governance and Matched Benchmarks | MLCommons-style working groups enforcing closed and open benchmark divisions across XR, CXL, and UCIe targets |
| Step 4 | Grand Challenges and Architecture Contests | Annual competitions at ISCA, MICRO, and DAC focused on timing closure, PPA optimization, and formal verification |
| Step 5 | Public Repositories of Failed Attempts | Shared logs of unroutable layouts, negative slack, UPF domain conflicts, and synthesis failures |
| Step 6 | University Curricula and Conference Badging | Cross-disciplinary university training and Autonomous Workflow Certified (AWC) badges |
: **Foundational schemas and signoff harnesses must exist before autonomous tools can produce comparable results.** The ordering forms the central argument of this chapter. This is a proposed sequence, not a program that has been run. {#tbl-ecosystem-staging-sequence}

When we trace this progression from Step 1 through Step 6, the initial two steps establish the pre-competitive physical substrate that makes reproducible exploration possible. Step 3 and Step 4 provide the consortium governance structures and competitive targets needed to align industrial and academic research teams. Step 5 and Step 6 complete the ecosystem by institutionalizing knowledge from failed design attempts and certifying workforce competencies.

The six execution steps group into a four-phase operational roadmap, read left to right from Phase 1 (Open Foundations) through Phase 2 (Consortium Governance) and Phase 3 (Acceleration and Audit) to Phase 4 (Scale and Sign-off), with a dashed feedback path linking public failure logs back to the foundations (@fig-ecosystem-roadmap).

![**Ecosystem staging establishes open foundations and neutral governance before scaling autonomous tools.** We execute ecosystem investments in four sequential phases (Phase 1 Open Data Schemas and PDK Shuttles, Phase 2 Consortium Governance and Matched Benchmarks, Phase 3 Grand Challenges and Public Failure Repositories, and Phase 4 Workforce Certification and Silicon Signoff). A dedicated feedback loop from public negative design attempts continuously calibrates surrogate models against physical feasibility boundaries.](images/fig-ecosystem-roadmap){#fig-ecosystem-roadmap width="100%" fig-alt="Left-to-right four-phase roadmap showing Phase 1 Open Foundations (Step 1 Schemas and Step 2 PDK Shuttles), Phase 2 Consortium Governance (Step 3 Closed/Open Divisions), Phase 3 Acceleration and Audit (Step 4 Contests and Step 5 Failure Repositories), and Phase 4 Scale and Certification (Step 6 Curricula and AWC Badging). A dashed feedback arrow connects negative design attempts back to the Phase 1 foundations."}

A defining architectural mechanism in @fig-ecosystem-roadmap is the dashed feedback loop connecting Step 5 back to the Phase 1 foundations. When public repositories capture unroutable placements, negative timing slack, and Unified Power Format (UPF) domain violations, this feedback continuously recalibrates our surrogate models against physical feasibility boundaries. If we attempt to deploy automated search or generative models without establishing Step 1 and Step 2, we risk creating unreproducible benchmarks, proprietary tool lock-in, and unverified candidate claims. Following this progression allows us to build each advance on evidence a third party can check. Whether the sequence works is itself an open question; nothing here has been run at ecosystem scale.

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Build open foundations before scaling autonomous tools"}
**The principle:** Scaling Architecture 2.0 across industry and academia requires open data schemas, pre-competitive physical signoff stacks, neutral consortium benchmarks, and public repositories of negative design attempts.

**The application:** Standardized contracts and verification harnesses must be established before deploying autonomous generation tools to ensure that AI-native hardware design remains open, auditable, and scientifically reproducible.
:::

## Shared Data Schemas and Tool Contracts {#sec-standardized-data-lineage}

The first step of our execution sequence addresses the root cause of fragmentation in modern AI-native design, which stems from a lack of interoperable data contracts. Today, our engineering teams often rely on custom JSON or YAML formats to record prompt sequences, simulator outputs, and physical layout metrics. Consequently, machine learning models trained in one environment fail to generalize when we transfer them to a different CAD flow or target technology node. When we release neutral, open specifications for decision contexts, attempt vectors, and tool execution logs, we enable cross-organizational knowledge transfer without exposing proprietary intellectual property.

To resolve this fragmentation, we look to how Accellera and IEEE 1666 (SystemC, an open system-level modeling standard based on C++) made system-level modeling interoperable by standardizing a common modeling language that commercial and open tools could both target [@IEEE2011SystemC1666]. Because formal standardization is deliberately slow (a standard that changes often is not one anyone can build against), an agile consortium (such as MLCommons or CHIPS Alliance) should fast-track a shared agent-interface specification, which we will call the Open Agentic Interface (OAI), before commercial EDA vendors establish locked, competing agent APIs. The proposal standardizes three core schemas.

- **Design problem formulations.** These provide explicit declarations of swept parameters, locked constraints, evaluation checks, and acceptance criteria ($s_{\text{design}}$). For example, in a mobile XR spatial accelerator exploration loop (@sec-architecture-20-ontology), the problem formulation defines architectural search bounds (such as PE array sizes $16\times16$ to $64\times64$ and SRAM capacity $256\text{ KB}$ to $2\text{ MB}$) and system obligations ($3\text{ W}$ Thermal Design Power limit and $120\text{ FPS}$ frame-rate obligation). It also declares target instruction sets (such as RISC-V RV64GCV), interconnect interfaces (such as UCIe and CXL), and target technology nodes (such as ASAP7 $7\text{ nm}$ open PDK alongside commercial TSMC N7 and N3 nodes).
- **Attempt lineage headers.** These supply cryptographically verifiable records linking candidate artifacts to their parent transformations, tool flags, structural representations, and environment configurations ($s_{\text{env}}$) [@SLSA2026Framework]. For example, when an AI generator modifies a SystemC Transaction-Level Modeling (TLM) memory controller or synthesizes a High-Level Synthesis (HLS) C++ kernel (@sec-data-representations-world-models), the lineage header records a cryptographic hash of the input prompt, parent git commit, Abstract Syntax Tree (AST), Control-Data Flow Graph (CDFG), MLIR/CIRCT Intermediate Representation (IR), container image digest (`arch2/tools@sha256:...`), random seed, Unified Power Format (UPF, IEEE 1801 standard) power state declarations, and CLI arguments. To protect corporate intellectual property, Schema 2 incorporates Zero-Knowledge Proof (ZKP) cryptographic commitments and selective disclosure schemes, allowing enterprise design teams to cryptographically assert candidate provenance without disclosing confidential microarchitectural structures or commercial foundry design rules.
- **Multi-fidelity environmental contracts and tool AI-readiness certification.** These specify typed schemas for input prerequisites, output guarantees, error bounds, and mandatory formal property checks across analytical models, cycle-level simulators, and Register-Transfer Level (RTL) synthesis tools. Certifying simulators and Electronic Design Automation (EDA) engines (such as gem5, Verilator, SCALE-Sim, Ramulator, OpenROAD, Yosys, and OpenSTA) as "AI-ready" ensures they expose deterministic container APIs, structured JSON-LD/protobuf state exports, fine-grained checkpoint recovery, machine-parsable error channels, and automated SystemVerilog Assertions with Bounded Model Checking (SVA/BMC) gatekeeping required for autonomous agent loops (@sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces). Mandatory formal verification gatekeeping prevents AI generators from logging candidates with hidden deadlock states or unverified timing exceptions into downstream lineage headers.

The proposed OAI specification binds these three schemas into one auditable data pipeline (@fig-oai-schemas). The three schema components sit side by side, and all converge on a single foundation, secure cross-organizational knowledge transfer.

![**The Open Agentic Interface (OAI) standardizes three core schemas to eliminate data fragmentation.** Design Problem Formulations declare search bounds and TDP obligations; Attempt Lineage Headers provide SLSA cryptographic provenance linking candidates to parent tool transformations; Multi-Fidelity Environmental Contracts certify simulators and EDA tools as AI-ready execution engines. Together they enable cross-organizational knowledge transfer without exposing proprietary foundry PDK parameters or confidential RTL.](images/fig-oai-schemas){#fig-oai-schemas width="100%" fig-alt="Diagram of the three core schemas of the Open Agentic Interface: Schema 1 Design Problem Formulation (swept bounds, TDP limit, target ISAs and nodes), Schema 2 Attempt Lineage Header (SLSA cryptographic hash, AST/CDFG representations, container image digest), and Schema 3 Environmental Contract (input preconditions, error bounds, AI-ready certified tools gem5, Verilator, OpenROAD, Yosys, OpenSTA). A pink bottom box shows cross-organizational knowledge transfer without exposing proprietary IP."}

The bottom layer of @fig-oai-schemas carries the point. When we adopt language-neutral specifications using Protocol Buffers or JSON-LD, design teams can safely exchange structured attempt traces across organizational boundaries, establishing a shared substrate for pre-trained hardware surrogates without exposing proprietary foundry PDK parameters or confidential RTL code.

## Open PDKs and Cloud Silicon Shuttles {#sec-precompetitive-infrastructure}

Even with standardized data schemas, autonomous exploration loops cannot validate physical feasibility without direct access to silicon signoff targets. Yet when we evaluate physical signoff constraints like wire-delay congestion, power-grid IR drop, UPF power domain boundary isolation, and dynamic thermal throttling, we traditionally encounter expensive commercial EDA licenses and restrictive non-disclosure agreements. As a result, most academic labs and startups cannot test their AI exploration algorithms against realistic physical targets.

We can bridge this divide by expanding open-source physical design infrastructure paired with cloud multi-project wafer shuttle services. Combining open PDKs (such as SkyWater $130\text{ nm}$ or ASAP7 $7\text{ nm}$) and predictive surrogates for leading-edge nodes (such as TSMC N7, N3, and N2 Gate-All-Around silicon) with open EDA frameworks (including OpenROAD, Yosys, OpenSTA, gem5, SCALE-Sim, and Ramulator) creates a fully functional, pre-competitive signoff flow. Predictive surrogates would learn transfer functions that bridge open PDK telemetry toward commercial physical phenomena, including multi-corner IR drop, electromigration, and dynamic thermal throttling in sub-3nm nodes. Whether such transfer holds at leading-edge nodes is itself unproven.

This model extends the classic MOSIS fabrication service (founded in 1981 at USC/ISI under DARPA sponsorship to democratize MPW shuttle access) [@MOSIS1981VLSI] and modern open shuttle aggregators (such as the Google SkyWater Open MPW program and Tiny Tapeout, an accessible open-silicon shuttle initiative) by establishing telemetry-sharing shuttle grants. To fund cloud silicon shuttles at scale ($5\text{M}$ to $10\text{M}$ USD annual funding pool), a public-private co-funding model (combining federal agencies like NSF, DARPA, and DOE with industrial consortium contributions) provides recurring access for competitive research teams. When we give autonomous AI design loops automated paths from AI-generated RTL directly to physical silicon measurements, we close the simulation-to-silicon gap. Standardized containerized environments allow us to evaluate our AI exploration algorithms on realistic physical targets without violating commercial software agreements.

## Consortium Governance and Matched Benchmarks {#sec-neutral-governance}

As open PDKs and cloud shuttles lower the barrier to physical verification, a new challenge emerges. We must ensure that published performance claims reflect genuine microarchitectural breakthroughs rather than benchmark over-optimization or uncalibrated baselines. Without neutral governance standards, our published AI hardware claims easily suffer from incomparable evaluation criteria. Authors select custom benchmarks, keep tuning parameters private, or compare their AI generator against weak baseline heuristics. When we establish multi-stakeholder consortia, we create objective evaluation standards that replace unverified marketing claims with rigorous microarchitectural verification.

Following the governance model established by MLCommons and MLPerf (the open benchmarking suite for machine learning hardware and systems), we should establish an independent Architecture Automation Working Group within established standards bodies (such as MLCommons, SPEC, CHIPS Alliance, or IEEE CEDA). Our working group must enforce three core responsibilities.

- **Reference problem suites.** We define reference problem suites grounded in realistic industrial constraints. These representative suites could cover $3\text{ W}$ mobile XR spatial processing, RISC-V RV64GCV vector clusters, datacenter tensor acceleration, CXL memory expansion, and UCIe chiplet interconnect management.
- **Closed and open benchmark divisions.** We establish a Closed Division where AI agents compete under strictly locked tool wrappers, fixed compute budgets, and identical baseline matching, alongside an Open Division that permits unconstrained search or proprietary surrogates provided authors report multi-dimensional workflow costs.
- **Total workflow cost accounting.** We mandate that published benchmarks account for the multi-dimensional resource vector ($C_{\text{workflow}} = \langle C_{\text{compute}}, C_{\text{license}}, C_{\text{human}} \rangle$), including GPU compute hours, EDA license checkout minutes, and human triage time.

## Grand Challenges and Architecture Contests {#sec-grand-challenges}

Once neutral governance structures establish rigorous evaluation rules, competitive grand challenges provide the forcing function needed to align community research on unsolved architectural bottlenecks. In computer architecture, community competitions have a rich heritage. Microarchitectural contests like the Championship Branch Prediction (CBP) [@CBP2016BranchPrediction], the Data Prefetching Championship (DPC) [@DPC2015DataPrefetching], and shared simulation frameworks like ChampSim [@GoberEtAl2022ChampSim] demonstrated how standardized trace benchmarks and open competition propel innovation in cache, prefetcher, and branch predictor design. Beyond microarchitecture, shared competition benchmarks catalyzed autonomous driving through the DARPA Grand Challenges [@BuehlerEtAl2009DARPA; @ThrunEtAl2006Stanley] and computer vision through ImageNet [@RussakovskyEtAl2015ImageNet]. Architecture 2.0 contests build directly upon this foundation, transitioning from hand-tuned human heuristics to closed-loop agentic exploration across three competition tracks, spanning physical synthesis, search efficiency, and adversarial verification.

- **Constrained physical PPA generation.** Candidates must yield timing-closed, area-efficient RTL from high-level specifications under strict power and thermal envelopes (such as our Lighthouse $3\text{ W}$ mobile XR accelerator prompt targeting TSMC N7 and N3 nodes from @sec-moonshot and @sec-intent-vs-spec). This track tests whether generative AI loops can achieve physical signoff feasibility without human intervention.
- **Sample-efficient space exploration.** Candidates must discover Pareto-optimal microarchitectural configurations for heterogeneous workloads (spanning RISC-V RV64GCV vector units and CXL memory topologies) under a strict simulation budget. This track tests whether search algorithms can navigate vast design spaces without wasting simulator cycles.
- **Adversarial red-teaming and hardware security.** Automated tools must identify latent timing exceptions, prompt-driven Trojan insertions, or verification loopholes in AI-generated hardware collateral using SystemVerilog Assertions and Bounded Model Checking (SVA/BMC) with explicit $k$-induction proof depth bounds ($k \ge 100$). This track tests whether verification harnesses can catch silent bugs before silicon commitment.

## Public Repositories of Failed Attempts {#sec-open-failed-attempts}

While competitive grand challenges highlight successful candidates, the true strength of autonomous search models depends equally on what they learn from failure. Today, our machine learning datasets suffer from severe survivorship bias because they consist almost exclusively of successful, timing-closed designs. As a result, surrogate models trained on these runs fail to recognize physical feasibility boundaries, frequently proposing candidates that violate routing density, AST/CDFG semantics, UPF power domain isolation, or power delivery rules. Public repositories of unroutable placements, negative-slack timing logs, and divergent tool runs supply the negative controls we need to train robust hardware surrogates.

When we create an anonymized, public repository of failed design attempts, we mirror practices in clinical medicine (such as ClinicalTrials.gov, the public registry for clinical research studies requiring negative trial outcome reporting) and aerospace safety (such as NTSB incident databases, the National Transportation Safety Board's accident record system). Learning from unroutable layouts, negative slack reports, and failed synthesis passes enables our AI models to predict physical signoff violations early in the design cycle. To realign academic incentives with public failure reporting, conference Artifact Evaluation Committees (AEC) and federal grant monitoring frameworks must make open negative attempt logging a prerequisite for paper badging and milestone disbursements.

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Build what makes other teams' claims checkable, not just your own"}
**The principle:** An individual team can make its own work reproducible and still leave the discipline unable to compare anything. Comparability is a property of the shared substrate, spanning open problem formulations, recorded costs, published failed attempts, and signoff access that does not depend on which contracts an organization holds.

**The application:** Invest in the substrate before scaling autonomous search across it, because a faster loop running on incomparable foundations produces results nobody outside the team can check. No team should wait for the consortium. Recording total cost and publishing what failed are practices that cost little and compound fastest when adopted.
:::

## University Curricula and Workforce Certification {#sec-workforce-certification}

Establishing open data contracts, physical signoff harnesses, and failure repositories provides the technical foundation for autonomous design, but infrastructure alone cannot transform an industry. Sustaining Architecture 2.0 at scale ultimately requires a workforce trained to audit, govern, and verify agentic workflows. Preparing our discipline for this responsibility demands that we align university education with peer-reviewed conference badging and enterprise signoff credentials.

Teaching students to manually write HDL code or hand-craft pipeline hazard units as the primary measure of competence is no longer sufficient for an era dominated by autonomous design loops. We must pivot university curricula toward four fundamental areas.

- **Prompt stack engineering.** Formal specification and multi-layer prompt stack design.
- **Autonomous verification.** Harness design and red-teaming methodologies.
- **Search space formulation.** Evaluator-driven search space formulation and Pareto trade-off synthesis.
- **Heterogeneous system integration.** Integration across CPU, NPU, memory, and packaging boundaries.

To address Bainbridge's irony of automation [@Bainbridge1983Ironies] and ensure human engineers retain primary operational agency rather than becoming the moral crumple zones of @sec-sustaining-responsibility [@Elish2019MoralCrumpleZones], our pedagogy must incorporate diagnostic laboratories. Students debug intentionally seeded cross-layer failures in agent-synthesized microarchitectures, developing deep physical intuition and diagnostic competence without incurring routine manual overhead. Students must also master open-to-commercial translation layers that map OpenROAD/Yosys telemetry to industrial Synopsys/Cadence signoff flows, ensuring academic research remains directly applicable to commercial tapeout teams.

In parallel, adopting established computational reproducibility standards [@Stodden2010ReproducibleResearch; @StoddenEtAl2016Science], conference Artifact Evaluation Committees (AEC) at venues like ISCA, MICRO, ASPLOS, and DAC should introduce explicit automated workflow badges. This badge certifies that an AI architecture study has published complete, machine-readable prompt histories, containerized execution logs, random seeds, and environmental contracts. Establishing these verification standards ensures that enterprise architecture teams satisfy auditability, baseline matching, and failure injection checks before committing capital to physical silicon tapeout.

## Ecosystem Outlook at Scale {#sec-ecosystem-outlook}

The outlook that follows is deliberately conditional. It describes what would change if the preceding steps succeed, not what current evidence establishes; the matched comparisons that would settle the underlying claims are exactly the ones @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect found missing. If curricula and badging institutionalize these verification standards and closed-loop exploration operates at industry scale, the bottlenecks of chip design migrate from manual execution to high-level system formulation, physical signoff governance, and multi-layer constraint trade-offs. That shift would run through four dimensions of our engineering discipline, spanning architect ownership, EDA industry structures, semiconductor economics, and global chip innovation.

### Architect Ownership and Skill Transformation

As automated design loops absorb the mechanics of RTL coding, physical floorplanning, and standard cell place-and-route sweeps, our primary contribution as architects shifts upstream and downstream. Upstream, we focus on formal problem framing, multi-layer prompt stack specification, objective function synthesis, and safety constraint boundary setting. Downstream, we govern residual risk, evaluate cross-layer trade-offs, and conduct adversarial red-teaming of AI recommendations.

We become design system architects who engineer both the hardware system and the autonomous loops that build it. We preserve technical contact not by manually editing gates, but by auditing agentic decision traces, inspecting failure counterexamples, and running independent verification checks. Our essential human responsibility remains unchanged. We must declare what the evidence supports, accept residual risk, and recommend commitments to authorized decision makers.

### EDA Industry Structures and Business Models

Beyond the individual architect, scaling autonomous workflows alters the software foundation of our discipline, namely the Electronic Design Automation (EDA) industry. Legacy EDA suites built around monolithic per-seat desktop GUI licenses are giving way to cloud-native, agentic API environments. We repurpose conventional EDA tools (synthesis compilers, static timing analyzers, formal verifiers, physical signoff engines) as headless execution tools and verification oracles within our agentic loops.

Open-source EDA infrastructures (such as OpenROAD, Yosys, OpenSTA, and Verilator) paired with AI search engines could reach parity with proprietary toolchains for a growing spectrum of SoC blocks. EDA business models would then shift from static per-seat annual licenses to compute-indexed or outcome-contingent pricing, where organizations pay based on design space exploration volume or verified PPA closure milestones.

### Semiconductor Economics and Capital Allocation

If agentic EDA environments compress front-end design cycles from years to weeks, the economic equations governing semiconductor investment realign. Automated exploration would lower the non-recurring engineering (NRE) labor cost for initial SoC design while leaving fixed physical capital costs, such as reticle mask sets, foundry shuttle runs, advanced 2.5D/3D packaging dies, and physical silicon validation, unaffected.

The economic bottleneck would then shift from front-end design labor to back-end physical mask fabrication and packaging yield, favoring hyper-specialized domain-specific ASICs. Custom chips for micro-verticals (such as edge XR, autonomous robotics, personalized medical devices, and localized AI inference) could become economically viable at low production volumes.

### Global Chip Innovation and Ecosystem Dynamics

When transformed pedagogical frameworks, open ISAs (such as RISC-V RV64GCV), open chiplet interconnect standards (such as UCIe), open memory standards (such as CXL), and accessible cloud compute converge, custom silicon creation could expand globally across diverse organizations. Hardware startups, regional research centers, and academic laboratories would gain the capability to design competitive, high-performance SoCs previously reserved for mega-cap semiconductor firms.

Hardware development could then track agile software release cycles, with silicon architectures iterating on quarterly or monthly schedules through modular chiplet updates and rapid automated design passes.

## Living Companion Infrastructure {#sec-living-web-hub}

Accelerating global hardware innovation and supporting agile design cadences cannot occur through static publications or fragmented repositories alone. To translate these macro transformations into daily engineering practice, our community requires a centralized, living infrastructure. We offer the companion hub concept for this book as a blueprint for community adoption rather than a claim of standing. A blueprint companion hub provides the following reference resources for readers, reviewers, and instructors.

- **Open Schema and Benchmark Registry.** Machine-readable Protocol Buffer and JSON-LD specifications for design problem formulations, attempt lineage headers, and environmental contracts.
- **Awesome-Architecture-2.0 Index.** A community-maintained, living directory categorizing papers, datasets, EDA tool wrappers, and AI agent frameworks across all six lifecycle stages.
- **Interactive Reviewer Audit Tool.** An online checklist implementing the verification rules from @sec-appendix-a-reviewer-checklist, enabling authors and conference reviewers to audit paper rigor prior to submission.
- **Dockerized Reference Starter Kits.** Containerized sandbox environments pre-configured with OpenROAD, Yosys, OpenSTA, gem5, Verilator, SCALE-Sim, Ramulator, UPF tools, and open PDKs (SkyWater $130\text{ nm}$ and ASAP7 $7\text{ nm}$) for immediate experimentation.

## Common Pitfalls {#sec-ecosystem-pitfalls}

Deploying a living web hub and containerized starter kits is only effective if the underlying tools, benchmarks, and training corpora remain active, unbiased, and physically calibrated. Without continuous stewardship and rigorous governance, shared infrastructure quickly degrades into abandoned code or vendor-locked silos. As we operationalize this open ecosystem, we must anticipate and actively mitigate four critical failure modes.

- **Open-Source Abandonware (unmaintained tool pipelines).** Relying on fragile, unmaintained academic research scripts without long-term industrial stewardship creates brittle synthesis loops.
- **Synthesizing Nonsense (hallucinated microarchitectural features).** Generating syntactically valid RTL that fails formal property verification or violates physical silicon rules degrades design trust.
- **Isolating Verification (fragmented telemetry and benchmarks).** Evaluating search algorithms on closed, proprietary workloads prevents reproducible cross-community comparison.
- **Ignoring Thermal and Power Constraints (unphysical designs).** Proposing speculative floorplans that violate thermal design power (TDP) or power delivery network (PDN) limits leads to unviable silicon candidates.

## Open Questions {#sec-ecosystem-open-questions}

Every chapter in this book has closed with questions rather than answers, and this one closes the device as well as the chapter. What we have laid out across these sections is not a complete research agenda, and it was never meant to be. The questions were chosen because we could see the shape of them from where the argument stood, which is a poor guarantee that they are the most important ones. Treat them as food for thought and as evidence that a discipline with open questions is a discipline that is still moving. The more useful exercise, once you close the book, is to write down the questions your own design problems raise that none of ours anticipated.

Maturing Architecture 2.0 raises research and policy questions that extend beyond near-term infrastructure bootstrapping. Resolving these open questions requires our community to pursue targeted technical and economic inquiries across three core dimensions.

**EDA tool architectures and agentic infrastructure.** Next-generation tooling must decouple generation from verification while maintaining open evaluation environments. Structuring robust interfaces ensures that autonomous design agents remain strictly accountable to independent verification oracles.

- **How should next-generation EDA infrastructures decouple generative synthesis agents from formal verification oracles?** A generator and a judge that share training heuristics can approve each other's mistakes, and no current tool architecture enforces the separation.
- **Can open-source EDA tools provide sufficient fidelity as fast evaluation oracles without requiring proprietary foundry process design kit (PDK) exposure?** The fidelity that matters is decision fidelity, whether the open-tool ranking of candidates survives commercial signoff, and that correlation remains largely unmeasured.

**Semiconductor economics and NRE governance.** Economic feasibility relies on quantitative gatekeeping and clear legal boundaries for generated code. Transitioning AI-native designs to commercial fabrication demands rigorous return-on-investment accounting and automated IP provenance tracking.

- **What metrics best evaluate whether an AI-proposed optimization justifies the fixed multi-million-dollar NRE mask cost of a leading-edge tapeout?** The projected gain arrives as a distribution over uncertain workloads while the mask charge is certain and immediate.
- **What static analysis and provenance-tracing algorithms can establish that AI-generated HDL does not infringe proprietary patent portfolios or violate licensing terms?** Similarity to protected designs is a legal judgment layered on a technical measurement, and neither layer has an accepted standard.

**Global chip innovation and agile hardware cadences.** Synchronizing hardware synthesis with rapid software releases demands democratized, versioned benchmarks. Aligning agile hardware cycles with production software deployments requires open infrastructure standards across global research ecosystems.

- **How can hardware organizations synchronize automated silicon synthesis loops with rapid software release cycles without compromising tapeout reliability?** Software can roll back a bad release; a mask set cannot.
- **What versioned benchmark infrastructures can objectively evaluate AI-driven design loops across global research organizations?** A benchmark that never changes gets gamed, and one that changes freely cannot support longitudinal claims.

## Summary {#sec-ecosystem-coda}

Decoupling logic design from physical silicon transformed computer architecture four decades ago by establishing scalable abstraction layers and standard design rules [@MeadConway1980VLSI]. Today, Architecture 2.0 presents an equivalent inflection point. Building a discipline-wide ecosystem for autonomous hardware exploration requires us to coordinate action across industry, academia, standards bodies, and tooling vendors. We must establish neutral data schemas, open physical signoff stacks, multi-stakeholder consortium benchmarks, and annual grand challenges to transform AI-native search from isolated corporate demonstrations into an open, auditable engineering discipline.

As we look to the future of our ecosystem, four core takeaways summarize our roadmap.

::: {.callout-takeaways title="Key Takeaways"}
- **Staged ecosystem sequence.** Ecosystem investments must proceed in strict order, establishing foundational data schemas and physical signoff harnesses before deploying autonomous generation tools.
- **Open data contracts.** Standardizing open specifications for design problem formulations, attempt lineage headers, and multi-fidelity tool contracts enables cross-organizational knowledge transfer.
- **Pre-competitive signoff infrastructure.** Combining open PDKs, cloud multi-project wafer shuttles, and containerized EDA toolchains closes the simulation-to-silicon gap for academic and industrial research.
- **Consortium governance and grand challenges.** Neutral working groups and annual competition tracks enforce rigorous baseline comparisons, total workflow cost accounting, and open artifact verification.
:::

The future of hardware design will not be written by locked, black-box generators or proprietary benchmarks. It will be built by an open community of architects, researchers, toolmakers, and domain experts working together to establish verifiable foundations for the next generation of computing. As we step into the era of Architecture 2.0, these shared foundations give AI deployment a path from isolated point assistance to a true AI-native design methodology, one that scales our expressible hardware complexity while preserving the rigor, auditability, and human accountability that define our discipline.
